title: Review: Homeostasis
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for IB Diploma Biology (review status in the bank: ai-specialist-reviewed-gate-verified-2026-09-21-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms: D3.3#c11, D3.3#c16, D3.3#c08, D3.3#c05. Clues: D3.3#c11 written for the game from the bank's definition; D3.3#c16 written for the game from the bank's definition; D3.3#c08 first sentence of the bank's definition; D3.3#c05 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: D3.3#q01, D3.3#q03, D3.3#q05, D3.3#q08, D3.3#q11, D3.3#q14, D3.3#q04, D3.3#q06, D3.3#q10, D3.3#q12, D3.3#q13, D3.3#q07. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Peripheral thermoreceptors
items.clue: Sensory cells in the skin that detect its temperature.

items.label: Shivering
items.clue: Rapid, involuntary muscle contractions that release heat.

items.label: Glycogen
items.clue: A branched polysaccharide of glucose stored as granules in liver and skeletal muscle cells.

items.label: Insulin
items.clue: A peptide hormone secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets when blood glucose concentration rises above the set point, for example after a meal.

questions.stem: Which statement about homeostasis in humans is correct?

options.text: Blood glucose concentration fluctuates within narrow preset limits around a set point.
Core body temperature is held at exactly 37 °C with no variation at all.
Skin temperature is kept within preset limits whatever the air temperature.
Blood pH is corrected only when it rises above its set point of about 7.4.

questions.explanation: Homeostasis maintains the internal environment by keeping variables such as blood glucose concentration within preset limits. The value is not fixed: it rises after a meal and falls during fasting, and negative feedback keeps these swings within a narrow range around the set point.

questions.stem: Why are homeostatic variables controlled by negative feedback rather than by positive feedback?

options.text: Negative feedback responds to harmful changes, while positive feedback responds to beneficial ones.
Negative feedback lowers a variable that has risen, which is the usual direction of deviation.
Negative feedback opposes a change, returning the variable towards its set point.
Negative feedback keeps the variable fixed at the set point with no fluctuation.

questions.stem: Blood glucose concentration rises after a meal. What happens next?

options.text: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets secrete insulin into the blood, and target cells take up more glucose.
The hypothalamus detects the rise and sends nerve impulses telling the pancreas to release insulin.
Insulin is released into the blood, where it breaks down the excess glucose molecules.
The pancreas secretes glycogen, which stores the excess glucose in the cells of the liver.

questions.stem: What is the physiological change that underlies type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Beta cells are destroyed by the immune system.
Beta cells are damaged by dietary sugar.
Insulin in the blood stops digesting glucose.
Target cells respond less to insulin.

questions.explanation: In type 2 diabetes insulin is secreted, at least in the early years, but liver, muscle and adipose cells have become insensitive to it, so glucose uptake falls and blood glucose stays high. This insulin resistance is why diet and exercise, which restore sensitivity, are the first treatments.

questions.stem: What is the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation?

options.text: It passes on the core temperature measured by thermoreceptors in the skin to the effectors.
It generates heat itself whenever the blood flowing through it becomes too cold.
It monitors blood temperature and coordinates the responses of the effectors.
It secretes thyroxin directly into the blood to raise the metabolic rate.

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus contains thermoreceptors that measure the temperature of the blood flowing through it and also receives impulses from peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin. It compares these with the set point and sends nerve impulses to effectors and hormonal signals via the pituitary gland.

questions.stem: On a hot, very humid day a runner sweats heavily, but their body temperature keeps rising. Why is sweating less effective in these conditions?

options.text: The sweat produced is warmer than usual, so it cannot chill the skin as it runs off.
Little of the sweat evaporates, so little latent heat is taken from the skin.
Humid air stops the blood vessels from moving up to the surface of the skin.
Sweat cools mainly as it drips off, and humid air makes it drip slowly.

questions.stem: During a long run, a person's blood glucose concentration falls to 3.5 mmol L−1. Glucagon secretion increases and the concentration returns to 5 mmol L−1. Which description of this sequence is correct?

options.text: Positive feedback, because the response raised the variable, not lowered it.
Positive feedback, because the response was beneficial and restored health.
A breakdown of homeostasis, because glucose left its set point of 5 mmol L−1.
Negative feedback correcting a fall of the variable below its set point.

questions.stem: Insulin is secreted into the blood, yet only cells such as liver, skeletal muscle and adipose cells respond to it. Why?

options.text: Insulin is carried by the blood directly to these organs and to no other part of the body.
Insulin reaches every tissue, but only these cells have receptors that bind it.
Insulin breaks down glucose only in tissues where glucose is concentrated.
The hypothalamus directs the insulin only to those organs that need it most.

questions.stem: Which change would do most to reduce a middle-aged adult's risk of developing type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Beginning insulin injections before any symptoms appear.
Reducing body fat through diet and regular physical activity.
Avoiding the viral infections thought to trigger loss of beta cells.
Taking enzyme supplements that digest glucose in the blood.

questions.explanation: Obesity, a diet rich in sugar and fat, and inactivity are the main modifiable risk factors for type 2 diabetes because they reduce the sensitivity of target cells to insulin. Losing fat and exercising restore sensitivity, so this is the prevention the guide expects.

questions.stem: A person moves to a cold climate. After several weeks their resting metabolic rate has risen and they produce more heat even when not shivering. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The pituitary gland is secreting thyroxin, which acts as quickly as a nerve impulse.
The hypothalamus has started to produce extra heat itself as the blood cools.
A thicker layer of white fat is making extra ATP, and the ATP is released as heat.
More thyroxin is being secreted, raising the rate of cell respiration.

questions.stem: How does vasodilation of the arterioles in the skin lower body temperature?

options.text: More blood flows through the capillaries near the surface, so more heat is lost to the air.
The blood vessels move closer to the surface of the skin, so heat escapes more easily.
Warm blood at the surface is cooled by the cold sweat that lies on top of the skin.
The capillaries contract their walls to squeeze warm blood towards the surface.

questions.explanation: Relaxation of smooth muscle in the arteriole walls widens them, so a greater volume of warm blood passes through the capillary beds close to the skin surface, where heat is transferred to the surroundings by radiation, conduction and convection.

questions.stem: Which option correctly pairs a hormone with its effect on target cells?

options.text: Glycogen: liver cells release glucose when its concentration in the blood falls too low.
Insulin: enzymes in the blood plasma digest glucose so that its concentration falls.
Glucagon: liver cells hydrolyse glycogen and release glucose into the blood.
Insulin: liver cells alone receive it, as the pancreas sends it there.

questions.explanation: Glucagon, secreted by alpha cells when blood glucose is low, binds to receptors on liver cells and stimulates the breakdown of stored glycogen to glucose, which is released into the blood to raise its concentration.
